\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{सैनिकः} (sainikaḥ)}{सैनिकः (sainikaḥ)}]{\sk{सैनिकः} (sainikaḥ) — a soldier}

\label{lesson:SA-C179-sainikah}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for a son-in-law, then the Sanskrit for a daughter-in-law.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{सैनिकः}}
\textbf{\sk{सैनिकः}} — \emph{sainikaḥ} — \textquotedblleft{}a soldier\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{sainika} is built on \emph{senā}, \textquotedblleft{}army\textquotedblright{}, with the suffix \emph{-ika}, \textquotedblleft{}belonging to\textquotedblright{} (MW): \textquotedblleft{}one who belongs to the army\textquotedblright{}. \emph{Senā} is the old word for \textquotedblleft{}army\textquotedblright{}, and it lives on as Hindi \emph{sen}, \textquotedblleft{}army\textquotedblright{} (CDIAL 13587).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for this chapter.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{sainikaḥ}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{sainikaḥ}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} say \emph{sainikaḥ}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Sanskrit for a son-in-law, then the Sanskrit for a daughter-in-law, then say \emph{sainikaḥ} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{सैनिकः} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}A soldier\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{रक्षकः} (rakṣakaḥ)}{रक्षकः (rakṣakaḥ)}]{\sk{रक्षकः} (rakṣakaḥ) — a guard}

\label{lesson:SA-C179-raksakah}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for a daughter-in-law, then the Sanskrit for a soldier.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{रक्षकः}}
\textbf{\sk{रक्षकः}} — \emph{rakṣakaḥ} — \textquotedblleft{}a guard\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{rakṣaka} is built on the root √rakṣ, \textquotedblleft{}to guard, protect\textquotedblright{}, with the agent suffix \emph{-aka} (MW): \textquotedblleft{}one who guards\textquotedblright{}. CDIAL 10545 records it as \textquotedblleft{}watchman\textquotedblright{}, and the verb \emph{rakṣati} lives on as Hindi \emph{rakhnā}, \textquotedblleft{}to keep\textquotedblright{} (CDIAL 10547).
\end{cousinweb}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{न्यायाधीशः} (nyāyādhīśaḥ)}{न्यायाधीशः (nyāyādhīśaḥ)}]{\sk{न्यायाधीशः} (nyāyādhīśaḥ) — a judge}

\label{lesson:SA-C179-nyayadhisah}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for a soldier, then the Sanskrit for a guard.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{न्यायाधीशः}}
\textbf{\sk{न्यायाधीशः}} — \emph{nyāyādhīśaḥ} — \textquotedblleft{}a judge\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{nyāyādhīśa} is a compound of \emph{nyāya}, \textquotedblleft{}rule, justice, judicial sentence\textquotedblright{}, and \emph{adhīśa}, \textquotedblleft{}lord, master\textquotedblright{} (MW). MW does not list the compound, so using it for a court judge is a modern pairing. \emph{Nyāya} is built on \emph{ni-} and the root √i, \textquotedblleft{}to go\textquotedblright{} (CDIAL 7614).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]

\end{grammarlens}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{अधिवक्ता} (adhivaktā)}{अधिवक्ता (adhivaktā)}]{\sk{अधिवक्ता} (adhivaktā) — a lawyer}

\label{lesson:SA-C179-adhivakta}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for a guard, then the Sanskrit for a judge.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{अधिवक्ता}}
\textbf{\sk{अधिवक्ता}} — \emph{adhivaktā} — \textquotedblleft{}a lawyer\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{adhivaktā} is the nominative of \emph{adhivaktṛ}, built on \emph{adhi-} and \emph{vaktṛ}, \textquotedblleft{}speaker\textquotedblright{}, from the root √vac, \textquotedblleft{}to speak\textquotedblright{}. MW already glosses it \textquotedblleft{}an advocate, protector\textquotedblright{}, the one who speaks up for you.
\end{cousinweb}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{लेखकः} (lekhakaḥ)}{लेखकः (lekhakaḥ)}]{\sk{लेखकः} (lekhakaḥ) — a writer}

\label{lesson:SA-C179-lekhakah}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for a judge, then the Sanskrit for a lawyer.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{लेखकः}}
\textbf{\sk{लेखकः}} — \emph{lekhakaḥ} — \textquotedblleft{}a writer\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{lekhaka} is built on the root √likh, \textquotedblleft{}to scratch, write\textquotedblright{}, which you have already met in \emph{likhati}, with the agent suffix \emph{-aka} (MW). It means \textquotedblleft{}scribe\textquotedblright{} (CDIAL 11102), and Hindi took it over unchanged as \emph{lekhak}.
\end{cousinweb}
